Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Eleanor, a 54-year-old chef with a reputation for precision and calm in the chaos of a professional kitchen, now finds herself a stranger in her own life. The assault occurred six months ago, not at the hands of a stranger in a dark alley, but in the familiar, spice-scented pantry of a man she had considered a friend for two decades. He had been hosting a small get-together, and she had offered to help. They were alone, discussing his recent separation, and Eleanor had offered a comforting hand on his arm. The conversation felt close, a moment of genuine connection. That, she now understands, was the beginning of the danger. The memory of what followed doesn't exist for her as a coherent story. It comes in jagged, sensory pieces: the rough texture of a burlap potato sack against her cheek, the overwhelming scent of dried oregano, the specific angle of afternoon light cutting through a high, dusty window. She cannot seem to put the core of the event into words, but when a fragment surfaces, her body remembers with perfect, terrifying clarity. She will be standing at her prep station at work and suddenly feel her spine curve and her arms instinctively cross over her chest, her body re-enacting the defensive position she was in on the pantry floor.

This fragmentation of memory has bled into her perception of the world. She has come to believe, with a certainty that feels absolute, that you can never truly know who might harm you. The betrayal by someone she trusted has become a universal law: people simply cannot be trusted. This conviction now governs her every interaction. In her kitchen, a world she once commanded with ease, she is perpetually on guard. A new line cook, a young man eager to please, becomes a source of profound unease. She avoids being in the walk-in freezer with him, sending her sous-chef instead. The sudden movement of a server rushing past her can cause her to flinch so violently she drops her knife. She feels threatened by the new delivery driver who brings the produce each morning, watching his every move from the corner of her eye until he leaves the premises. Her staff, once fiercely loyal, now see a woman who is distant and unpredictable.

At home, the space she shares with her husband has become a landscape of invisible tripwires. He has learned not to approach her from behind. When he reaches out to hold her, that simple gesture of emotional closeness feels like a precursor to harm, and she stiffens, pulling away. Any conversation that touches on themes of disappointment or broken promises—a friend letting him down, a politician’s empty pledge—is unbearable for Eleanor. She will abruptly change the subject or leave the room, unable to tolerate the echoes of her own betrayal. He sees her distress but cannot reach her; she has no language for the terror that keeps her locked away, even from him.

The decision to seek therapy came after a particularly frightening incident at the restaurant. During a chaotic dinner service, a busboy dropped a stack of plates. The sudden crash sent a bolt of panic through Eleanor, so intense she felt she was back in the pantry. She stumbled backward, gasping for air, her vision tunneling. Her sous-chef had to grab her arm to steady her, his touch feeling like another threat. Seeing the mixture of fear and confusion on the faces of her young staff, she realized she could no longer manage the storm inside her. She is terrified that this hyper-alert, isolated version of herself is who she is now, permanently. More than anything, Eleanor hopes to reclaim a sense of safety in the world, to be able to stand in her own kitchen or her own home without feeling like a target.
